title: How Often Should You Get a Dental Cleaning?
seoTitle: How Often Should You Get a Dental Cleaning? Arlington Guide
seoDescription: Most patients need a dental cleaning every 6 months, but gum health, buildup, medical history, and orthodontic treatment can change the right schedule. Learn when to book sooner.
author: Sonria Dentista clinical team
summary: A practical guide to dental cleaning frequency: who usually needs cleanings every six months, who may need visits every three or four months, what happens if you wait too long, and how Arlington patients can choose the right preventive care schedule.
heroImageAlt: Dental hygienist preparing preventive cleaning instruments for a patient visit

body.text: For many patients, the simple answer is that you should get a dental cleaning every six months. That twice-a-year schedule works well for people with healthy gums, light to moderate tartar buildup, and no recent history of active gum disease. It gives your dental team enough time to remove hardened plaque before it causes bigger problems and to catch small cavities, cracked fillings, gum inflammation, or bite changes before they become painful or expensive.

But six months is not a rule for every mouth. Some patients do better with cleanings every three or four months, especially if they have periodontal disease, heavy buildup, dry mouth, diabetes, tobacco use, crowded teeth, braces, clear aligners, or a history of frequent cavities. Other patients with excellent home care and low risk may still stay on a six-month schedule because dental cleanings are not only about polishing teeth. They are also a regular checkpoint for oral cancer screening, gum measurements, bite changes, restoration checks, and prevention planning.
The Standard Schedule: Every Six Months

A cleaning every six months is the standard preventive schedule because plaque can harden into tartar even when you brush and floss consistently. Once plaque becomes tartar, it cannot be removed with a toothbrush or floss at home. A hygienist removes it with professional instruments, then polishes the tooth surfaces so they feel smooth and are easier to keep clean.

At Sonria Dentista, a routine preventive visit usually includes a review of your medical history, gum health screening, professional cleaning, polishing, and dentist exam when appropriate. X-rays are recommended based on your risk level, symptoms, and how long it has been since your last images. The goal is not to over-treat. The goal is to keep a small issue from turning into an emergency appointment.
Who May Need Cleanings Every Three or Four Months?

Some patients collect plaque and tartar faster than others. The right cleaning interval depends on what your gums and teeth show over time, not just the calendar. If your gums bleed easily, pockets are deeper than normal, or tartar returns quickly after each visit, your dentist may recommend a shorter recall schedule.

body.text: A three- or four-month schedule is not a punishment and it does not mean you are doing everything wrong at home. It often means your mouth has risk factors that need closer maintenance. For patients who have already had gum therapy, more frequent maintenance can help protect the bone and gum support around teeth.
What If You Have Not Had a Cleaning in Years?

If it has been a few years since your last cleaning, the first visit may not be a simple polish. Your dental team needs to check for tartar under the gumline, gum pocket depths, bone changes, cavities, broken fillings, and infection. Some patients can restart with a regular cleaning. Others may need a deeper cleaning, often called scaling and root planing, if gum disease is present.

The most important step is to come in before discomfort forces your hand. Delaying because you are embarrassed usually makes the next appointment harder, not easier. Dental teams see delayed care every day, and a good preventive visit should focus on a clear plan, not blame.
How Cleanings Help Prevent Bigger Dental Costs

Professional cleanings are one of the simplest ways to reduce the risk of larger dental bills. Tartar and inflamed gums can contribute to periodontal disease, which may require more involved treatment and ongoing maintenance. Small cavities that are found early may be treated with a filling, while untreated decay can lead to crowns, root canals, extractions, or dental implants.

A cleaning visit also gives your dentist a chance to check older dental work. Crowns, bridges, fillings, veneers, and implants all need regular monitoring. Catching a loose crown margin, cracked filling, or bite problem early can protect the tooth structure you still have.
Dental Cleaning Frequency by Patient Type

For a low-risk adult with healthy gums and good home care, every six months is usually appropriate. For a patient with gingivitis, heavy buildup, or inconsistent flossing, the dentist may suggest improving home care and returning sooner to see if inflammation improves. For periodontal disease, cleanings may shift to periodontal maintenance every three or four months after active treatment.

Children and teens also need consistent preventive visits. Six-month cleanings help monitor tooth eruption, bite development, cavities, sports-related tooth risk, and hygiene around orthodontic appliances. Older adults may need closer care if dry mouth, medications, dexterity changes, gum recession, or restorations make daily cleaning harder.
Signs You Should Schedule a Cleaning Sooner

Do not wait for your next scheduled cleaning if something feels off. Bleeding gums, swollen gums, tooth sensitivity, bad breath that does not improve, visible tartar, a rough feeling near the gumline, a loose tooth, or pain when chewing are all reasons to call. These signs do not always mean something serious, but they are worth checking before they become urgent.

Patients in Arlington, Grand Prairie, Mansfield, Pantego, and nearby communities can use a cleaning visit as a starting point for a practical plan. If your mouth is healthy, you will know what to keep doing. If there is inflammation or buildup, your dentist can explain the next step and the timing that fits your risk.
How to Keep Your Cleaning Schedule on Track

Brush twice daily with fluoride toothpaste, clean between teeth once daily, and ask your hygienist to show you the spots you tend to miss. If floss is difficult, interdental brushes, floss picks, or a water flosser may be more realistic. The best home-care routine is the one you can repeat consistently.

Before you leave your appointment, schedule the next cleaning. It is easier to protect time on your calendar now than to remember six months later. If insurance benefits are part of your decision, ask the team to help you understand preventive coverage, frequency limitations, and whether periodontal maintenance is handled differently than a routine cleaning.

FAQ
Is a dental cleaning every six months really necessary?

For most patients, yes. Six-month cleanings help remove tartar, monitor gum health, catch cavities early, and keep preventive care predictable. Your dentist may recommend a different schedule if your risk is higher or lower.
Can I get my teeth cleaned more often than twice a year?

Yes. Patients with gum disease, heavy tartar buildup, dry mouth, diabetes, tobacco use, or orthodontic appliances may benefit from cleanings every three or four months. Your dentist should explain why a shorter interval is recommended.
What happens if I skip dental cleanings?

Skipping cleanings allows tartar to build up and can make gum inflammation, cavities, bad breath, and tooth sensitivity more likely. Small problems may also go unnoticed until they require more involved treatment.
Do dental cleanings hurt?

A routine cleaning should not be painful, though sensitive gums or heavy buildup can make parts of the visit uncomfortable. Tell your hygienist if you feel sensitivity so the team can adjust technique and discuss options.
